title: The Day Boston Drowned in Molasses
creator: The Archive Hour
description:
In January 1919 a storage tank in Boston's North End burst and sent a wave of molasses through the streets. Twenty-one people died. This is what happened, and what changed because of it.

Sources:
Stephen Puleo, Dark Tide: The Great Boston Molasses Flood of 1919
Boston Public Library digital archive, newspaper scans Jan-Feb 1919
Massachusetts court records, Dorr v. United States Industrial Alcohol

Suggest a topic in the comments.

sentences.t: So that's the story of the Great Molasses Flood, and honestly I still find it hard to say that phrase with a straight face.
But twenty-one people died that January afternoon in Boston, and around a hundred and fifty were hurt.
A wave of molasses, something like twenty-five feet high at its peak, came down Commercial Street at about thirty-five miles an hour.
It flattened buildings, it buckled the steel supports of the elevated railway, and it trapped horses and people in a substance that got thicker as it cooled.
Rescuers waded in up to their waists, and some of the victims weren't found for days.
Now, the part I keep coming back to is what happened afterwards.
The company that owned the tank, United States Industrial Alcohol, insisted the tank had been blown up by anarchists.
That wasn't a crazy thing to claim in 1919, because bombings really were happening, and the company knew a jury might believe it.
But the case dragged on for years, and the court-appointed auditor heard from something like three thousand witnesses.
And what came out was pretty damning.
The tank had been built in a hurry, it had never been properly tested by filling it with water, and it leaked so badly that the company painted it brown to hide the streaks.
Locals used to collect the leaking molasses in buckets and take it home.
In the end the company was found responsible and paid out the equivalent of millions in today's money.
More importantly, the case pushed Massachusetts, and later other states, to require that engineers actually sign off on structures like this.
So in a strange way, every certified engineer's stamp on a building plan has a little bit of molasses in its history.
People in the North End will tell you that on hot summer days, the neighborhood still smelled sweet decades later.
I can't verify that, but I love that it's the kind of detail that just refuses to go away.
If you want to read more, the best book on this is Dark Tide by Stephen Puleo, and I've put a few other sources in the description.
